task.name: What an issue cost across all its attempts is never reported, so the figure that should decide whether to re-run it is the one an operator cannot see
task.story_text:
## Why

Every cost an operator is shown is scoped to a run. What an issue cost to land is never reported
anywhere, and for the issues that matter most it is the only figure that describes what happened.

An issue that fails, is preserved, and is re-entered accrues spend across several runs. Each run
reports its own total honestly, and the per-run records sum correctly — the arithmetic is sound.
What is missing is the sum. Status output, sprint summaries and the RCA all stop at the run
boundary, so the number that answers "what did this issue cost" exists only by querying the audit
substrate directly.

The gap is not evenly distributed. Measured over roughly two weeks of this project's own history:

```
runs to land   issues   avg total   sum
     1           80      $12.61     $1,008.95
     2           12      $19.35       $232.22
     3+           4     $117.43       $469.71
```

17% of issues needed more than one run and consumed 41% of all spend. Four issues — 4% of the work —
accounted for 27% of the total. An issue needing three runs costs roughly nine times one that lands
first time.

None of that is visible while it is happening. The largest single one reached $341 across five runs,
and the biggest figure ever displayed for it was $169.94, on a screen that described a run rather
than the issue. An operator watching per-run costs sees numbers that look survivable while the
actual commitment compounds out of view, and the decision that figure should inform — keep re-running
this, or stop and re-scope it — is exactly the decision being made without it.

The routing layer already reasons in these terms: a story allocation is derived from historical
per-story cost, and escalation messages quote medians and percentiles over prior runs. So the
aggregate exists internally as an input to automated decisions. It is simply never surfaced to the
person paying for it.

## Example

What is shown today while an issue is re-entered for the fifth time, and what is not:

```
shown                                   not shown
─────────────────────────────────       ──────────────────────────────
run 7b995cfaaa5f   $137.69              issue total        $341.10
elapsed 2h 43m                          runs to date             5
sprint total       $166.81              elapsed, all runs   ~9h 20m
                                        outcomes    RC, APPROVE, RC, killed, escalated
```

Wanted: at the point an issue is re-entered, and in any summary that names it, the figure for the
issue alongside the figure for the run — so a fifth attempt is visibly a fifth attempt, and its
running total is on screen when the decision to make it is taken.

## Acceptance criteria

- A surface that names an issue reports what that issue has cost across every run that worked on it,
  not only the run being displayed, so the aggregate never has to be reconstructed by hand.
- The aggregate counts each run's spend once. Where a run already carries spend forward from an
  earlier attempt, the total reflects what was spent, not the sum of figures that overlap.
- Where any run contributing to the total recorded unmeasured spend, the aggregate says so rather
  than presenting a total that silently understates itself.
- The count of attempts is reported with the cost, so an operator can tell a single expensive attempt
  from several cheap ones, which call for different responses.
- An issue re-entered after a previous attempt has its running total available at the point of
  re-entry, before the new attempt spends anything.
- An issue that has only ever run once reads the same as it does today, so the common case gains a
  figure rather than changing meaning.

## Out of scope

Changing what is spent, or how allocation is derived from history. This is a reporting gap: the
records already exist and already sum correctly. Also out of scope is recording what a run changed
as opposed to what it cost, which is tracked separately.

handoff.summary: Added a read-only cross-run issue cost aggregate and threaded it into every surface that names an issue. `audit_substrate.issue_cost_aggregate()` gathers per-story run records by slug or issue id, merging in canonical `.forge/audits/runs/*.json` payloads the index has not caught up with (probed cheaply via indexed source_path/source_mtime so an up-to-date substrate parses nothing). It drops an ancestor run from the sum when a descendant's `prior_generation` block shows the cost was carried forward, keeps a measured lower bound via a new public `unmeasured.measured_lower_bound()` when a contributing run never measured its spend, excludes sprint rollup records, and supports `exclude_run_id` for pre-spend disclosure. `sprint/issue_cost.py` is the single loader/formatter (IssueCostLoader opens one connection per render; IssueCostSummary serializes the `issue_cost` YAML block; format_issue_cost is silent for single-attempt issues). Consumers: StoryStatusEntry.issue_cost populated in read_live_status/read_completed_status (with the persisted row as fallback), rendered by cli/sprint_status._print_story_line; `_disclose_reentry_costs()` called in run_sprint after story resolution and before the ThreadPoolExecutor; `_attach_issue_cost_rows()` stamping summary and accumulated rows; digest `_story_row` and the OUTSTANDING section; RCA `cost_accounting`; batch report dataclass/payload/terminal. Every path is best-effort — absent substrate behaves exactly as before.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: A surface that names an issue reports what that issue has cost across every run that worked on it, not only the run being displayed, so the aggregate never has to be reconstructed by hand.
acceptance_criteria.notes: Sprint status story lines, the postmortem digest story rows and OUTSTANDING section, sprint-summary story rows, sprint RCA cost_accounting, and the batchability report all carry the aggregate. All derive from one helper over canonical per-run records.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: The aggregate counts each run's spend once. Where a run already carries spend forward from an earlier attempt, the total reflects what was spent, not the sum of figures that overlap.
acceptance_criteria.notes: _carries_parent_spend() drops an ancestor from the sum only when the descendant's prior_generation block records independently_recorded=False and 'cost' in carried_keys — the exact condition under which sprint.audit.carry_prior_generation_work folded the parent's cost block in. Sprint rollup records are excluded for the same reason. Regression tests cover both the overlapping and the independently-recorded (disjoint) parent/child shapes.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: Where any run contributing to the total recorded unmeasured spend, the aggregate says so rather than presenting a total that silently understates itself.
acceptance_criteria.notes: cost_complete goes False when any contributing run's total is null; the run still contributes its measured agent costs as a floor via unmeasured.measured_lower_bound(). Every renderer words it as 'issue total at least $X ... (some spend was never measured)'.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: The count of attempts is reported with the cost, so an operator can tell a single expensive attempt from several cheap ones, which call for different responses.
acceptance_criteria.notes: attempts counts distinct contributing runs and is rendered in every wording. A run whose spend a descendant carries forward is excluded from the sum but still counted as an attempt — it was a run that worked on the issue.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: An issue re-entered after a previous attempt has its running total available at the point of re-entry, before the new attempt spends anything.
acceptance_criteria.notes: _disclose_reentry_costs() runs in run_sprint after story resolution and before the ThreadPoolExecutor — the single choke point detached and re-exec'd resumes both re-enter through. It excludes the current run_id and words the figure as prior-attempt spend so it cannot be read as the attempt now starting. An AST-level test pins the call site upstream of the executor so a later change cannot silently move it after dispatch.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: An issue that has only ever run once reads the same as it does today, so the common case gains a figure rather than changing meaning.
acceptance_criteria.notes: format_issue_cost returns empty below 2 attempts, so single-attempt rows and legacy summaries without the issue_cost block render byte-identically. Pinned by tests on both the status story line and the digest row.

plan_review.findings:
- [P1-impl] [anthropic-opus-cli] Step 1 puts a canonical-JSON freshness check and fallback inside audit_substrate, but does not say what 'newest matching canonical run' means when a story's runs live under multiple slugs/issue ids — .forge/audits/runs/*.json is a flat directory keyed by run_id, so identifying matching records requires reading payloads rather than a filename or index lookup, which is O(all runs) on every status render.
  Suggestion: Scope the freshness probe cheaply (e.g. compare newest runs-dir mtime against the newest indexed started_at, and only parse payloads when that comparison indicates the index lags), so status rendering does not scan the full run corpus each time.
- [P1-impl] [anthropic-opus-cli] Step 4 lists both src/theforge/cli/sprint.py and src/theforge/sprint/runner.py as the disclosure site without choosing one; sprint.py has several resume-carrying entry points (lines 244, 306, 383, 1183, 1236, 1317), so a disclosure added at one of them can be bypassed by the others (detached/re-exec paths).
  Suggestion: Pick the single choke point that every resumed story passes through after story resolution and before dispatch, and assert in the integration test that the detached/re-exec resume path also emits it.
- [P2] [anthropic-opus-cli] Steps 4 and 7 name tests/test_cli_sprint_resume.py and tests/test_issue_cost_reporting.py under 'modify'; neither file exists today (tests/ has test_cli_status.py and test_reentry_disclosure.py but no sprint-resume or issue-cost module).
  Suggestion: Treat those as new files, or place the resume-disclosure test alongside the existing sprint resume coverage so it runs with the related suite.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules

Keep modules single-purpose. Extract when a responsibility separates from its neighbours — never to satisfy a line count. Putting a change in an already-large module is correct if that is where it belongs; a module carved at whatever line got the count down is worse than the large module it came from.
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.
